title: Do bond builders repair disulfide bonds? A science blogger's critique of a 2024 bleached-hair study
headline: A commentary post (16 Oct 2026) argues the 2024 study used to support Olaplex's mechanism used the wrong test for the bonds it claims; the underlying work used bleached hair, not tightly coiled hair.
evidenceTier: Commentary page read (via fetch summary); primary 2024 study not opened by me
fit: Hair-care claims context: it weakens the mechanism story behind bond-builder marketing, and says nothing about tightly coiled, high-porosity hair, which was not studied.
displaces: Nothing to add; if a bond-builder step exists, this is a reason to judge it by results on your own hair, not by the mechanism claim.
estimateNote: Prices marked EST are my guesses, not looked up.
summaryPoints: Commentary (Lab Muffin, 16 Oct 2026; read through a fetch summary, not the full post): analyses Martins et al., Cosmetics 2024, which treated bleached hair with Olaplex No.0 and K18 (10% w/w, leave-in) and measured thiols with Ellman's test and disulfides with Raman spectroscopy.

The post's criticism: the study read Ellman's test (with borohydride) as evidence of new sulfur-sulfur-carbon bonds, but the test mostly detects disulfides; conditions differed between runs; so the study does not support the patent's proposed mechanism. The post's verdict is the author's opinion, labelled as such.
Frame: bleached hair of unstated origin was the template; tightly coiled (3C to 4B), high-porosity hair was not studied. Funding for the 2024 study was not stated in the post.
Follows the 25 Oct run's entry on a curl shampoo from the same brand: no change to the verdict there.
toneData: Not applicable (bleached hair samples; hair type not specified)
fitLine: Hair texture was not studied; useful only as a lens on marketing claims.
